title: Coin Change
keyIdea: dp[x] = fewest coins that make x. The last coin used is one of the coins, so dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x − coin]) over coins that fit; dp[0] = 0, and INT_MAX means x can't be made. Greedy (biggest coin first) is wrong.

approaches.name: Memoization
approaches.idea: Your solve(amount): try every coin that fits as the last coin, ask solve(amount − coin), keep the smallest 1 + answer; save it in dp so each amount is solved once.
approaches.why: amount + 1 states, each trying k coins once. dp has amount + 1 entries and the recursion can go amount deep (all 1-coins).

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: Your active code: dp[0] = 0; for i = 1..amount, mini over coins ≤ i of 1 + dp[i − coin] (skipping INT_MAX); dp[i] = mini. INT_MAX at the end → -1.
approaches.why: Two nested loops: amount values × k coins, O(1) work each. One array of amount + 1, no recursion.

quiz.q: Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6. What does greedy (biggest first) give, and what is right?
Why check temp != INT_MAX before adding 1?
options: INT_MAX means that amount can't be made, and 1 + INT_MAX would overflow
-1: odd amounts can't be made from 2s
